prompt: Which half of an access key may appear in a log or a ticket without harm?
hint: One half names the key; the other signs with it.

choices.text: The secret access key, since it is never sent with a request
choices.why: It is never sent because it is the part that signs. Whoever reads it can sign as the user.

choices.text: The access key id, `AKIA…`
choices.why: Right. It names the key and is in every request and every CloudTrail line; on its own it signs nothing.

choices.text: Neither: both halves are equally secret
choices.why: The id is not secret at all. Treating it as one makes a CloudTrail search impossible to share.

choices.text: Either half, as long as the other stays hidden
choices.why: The secret alone is enough to sign once the id is guessed or found, and the id is printed everywhere.

prompt: A secret access key is forty characters long. Why is that length no defence in practice?
hint: How do keys reach attackers?

choices.text: Because AWS only checks the first sixteen characters
choices.why: The whole secret goes into every signature. The length is real; it just protects against the wrong attacker.

choices.text: Because modern hardware can try every forty-character string
choices.why: Nothing can try them all. That is exactly why nobody attacks a key by guessing.

choices.text: Because keys are copied from where they were written, never guessed
choices.why: Right. A key found in a repository, an image or a log works whatever its length.

choices.text: Because the id tells an attacker most of the secret
choices.why: The id and the secret are independent strings. One says nothing about the other.

prompt: Match each caller to what it should use instead of an access key.
hint: The section's table of alternatives.

pairs.right: IAM Identity Center and `aws sso login`
its OIDC token, traded for a role

pairs.left: an office server with a certificate

right_distractors: a second access key, rotated monthly

prompt: Which of these are ways keys leak, as the section describes them? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three are copies made by ordinary tools.

choices.text: A `.env` committed once and removed in the next commit
choices.why: Right. The first commit still holds it, and a public repository is scanned within minutes.

choices.text: An image built with `COPY . .` from a directory holding `~/.aws`
choices.why: Right. Every layer can be unpacked by anyone who can pull the image.

choices.text: A CI job running with `set -x`
choices.why: Right. The shell prints each command with its variables expanded, keys included, into the job's log.

choices.text: An attacker trying secret strings until one signs correctly
choices.why: Nobody leaks a key that way; the number of strings is far beyond any attempt.

choices.text: AWS printing the secret in CloudTrail
choices.why: CloudTrail records the key id. The secret is never sent, so AWS has nothing to print.

prompt: A developer pushes a key to a public repository and removes it in a second push ten minutes later. What should happen to the key?
hint: What does a commit keep?

choices.text: Nothing more: it was public for only ten minutes
choices.why: Scanners read public pushes within minutes, and the first commit still holds the key after the second push.

choices.text: Treat it as leaked: deactivate it, look at what it did, rotate
choices.why: Right. The second push changed the latest version, not the history, and the key has to be assumed copied.

choices.text: Rewrite the repository's history so the commit disappears, and keep the key
choices.why: Rewriting history removes the evidence, not the copies already made of it.

choices.text: Make the repository private
choices.why: That stops future readers, not the ones who read it in those ten minutes.

prompt: How many access keys may one IAM user have at the same time?
hint: moto refused the next one with `LimitExceeded`.

prompt: Put the steps of rotating `erp-sync`'s key in order.
hint: Every step but the last can be undone.
items: move the program to the new key
check that the old key's last use stopped moving
wait, then delete the old key
trap: Deleting comes last because it is the one step that cannot be taken back.

prompt: Why is the old key made `Inactive` and left for a while, rather than deleted as soon as the program has switched?
hint: What happens to whatever still used it?

choices.text: Because a key cannot be deleted while it is `Active`
choices.why: An active key can be deleted at once; the order is a choice, not a rule IAM enforces.

choices.text: So a forgotten user fails while the key is recoverable
choices.why: Right. `--status Active` undoes the switch-off in one command; nothing undoes a deletion.

choices.text: Because AWS needs a week to remove the key from its systems
choices.why: A deleted key stops working straight away, as moto showed with `InvalidAccessKeyId`.

choices.text: So that the credential report has time to record the rotation
choices.why: The report is generated on request and shows the change the next time it is.

prompt: A day after the accounting system moved to the new key, the old key's `LastUsedDate` is still changing. What does it mean, and what comes next?
hint: Who else holds the old pair?

choices.text: Nothing: the date updates on its own once a day
choices.why: The date moves only when a request is signed with the key. Something signed with it.

choices.text: The new key failed, so delete it and keep the old one
choices.why: The new key's own date says whether it works. The old date moving says somebody else exists.

choices.text: Another program uses it; find that before the switch-off
choices.why: Right. Finding that user is the reason the old key was not deleted yet, and its CloudTrail lines say where it calls from.

choices.text: The key has leaked, so delete the user
choices.why: It may be a forgotten script rather than an intruder, and deleting the user removes both keys and the evidence.

prompt: In the lab, the old key uploaded successfully after `update-access-key --status Inactive`. What does that establish?
hint: Recorded is not enforced.

choices.text: Only that moto records `Inactive` and goes on accepting the key
choices.why: Right. AWS refuses every request signed with an inactive key, which is the failure the step exists to provoke.

choices.text: That `Inactive` takes effect only after the next credential report
choices.why: The report reads the state; it does not apply it. In AWS the refusal is immediate.

choices.text: That an inactive key still works for S3 but not for other services
choices.why: Nothing in the lab compared services, and AWS documents no such exception.

choices.text: That the policy `upload-erp` overrides the key's status
choices.why: A policy decides what a valid key may do. An inactive key is not valid at all in AWS.

prompt: The credential report arrives in base64, so it is read with `aws iam get-credential-report --query Content --output text | base64 ___`.
hint: The option that decodes.

prompt: `key-ages.py` prints `old-report  key 1  400 days  last used N/A  ROTATE`. What should happen to that key?
hint: Read the last-used column as well as the age.

choices.text: Rotate it, as the flag says
choices.why: Rotating gives a key nobody uses a fresh replacement. The flag counts days; the empty last use says more.

choices.text: Switch it off, wait, delete it; no new key
choices.why: Right. A key never used in 400 days is a key to remove; switching it off first still catches a surprise.

choices.text: Leave it: a key never used cannot leak
choices.why: It can leak exactly like any other, and then its first use is the intruder's.

choices.text: Attach the quarantine policy to it
choices.why: Nothing says it leaked. The quarantine is for a key found in public, not for one that is merely old.

prompt: Past how many days does `key-ages.py` flag a key, the line the CIS benchmark and Security Hub's `IAM.3` draw?
hint: The value of `LIMIT`.

prompt: Why does `mfa-to-delete.json` use `BoolIfExists` rather than `Bool`?
hint: What does a request signed with the key alone carry?

choices.text: Because `Bool` cannot compare against `false`
choices.why: `Bool` compares against either value. The issue is a key that is not there at all.

choices.text: Key-only requests lack that key, and `Bool` would miss them
choices.why: Right. The deny would skip exactly the request it exists for; `IfExists` makes the absent key count as a match.

choices.text: Because `IfExists` makes the policy apply in every region
choices.why: Regions have nothing to do with it; `IfExists` is about a missing condition key.

choices.text: Because moto only understands the `IfExists` forms
choices.why: moto ignores conditions altogether, as the flipped test showed. The choice follows AWS's evaluation.

prompt: With the condition inverted to deny only requests that DO have MFA, moto still refused `dani`'s key-only delete. What follows?
hint: In AWS that delete would have been allowed.

choices.text: That an explicit deny always wins, whatever its condition says
choices.why: In AWS a deny applies only when its condition matches. This one did not, and AWS would allow the delete.

choices.text: That `dani`'s key carries MFA without her knowing
choices.why: A key never carries MFA; only a session from `get-session-token` with a code does.

choices.text: That moto ignores the condition, so the first refusal proved nothing about it
choices.why: Right. A deny with a condition denies always in moto; whether the MFA condition matches is AWS's documented behaviour.

choices.text: That `AmazonS3FullAccess` leaves out `s3:DeleteObject` for buckets that hold backups
choices.why: It does: `s3:*`. The refusal came from the inline deny, which moto applied unconditionally.

prompt: A key is found in a public gist. Put the response in order.
hint: Stop it first; understand it before replacing it.
items: search CloudTrail for what the key id did
undo what it created, sessions included
give the program a new key and delete the old
trap: Rotating before investigating replaces the key while whatever the intruder made is still there.

prompt: AWS attaches `AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3` to a user whose key it found in public. What is still left to do?
hint: A brake, not a cure.

choices.text: Nothing: the policy deactivates the key
choices.why: It leaves the key active and denies a list of actions. The key still signs everything the list misses.

choices.text: Only removing the policy once the user confirms it was a mistake
choices.why: A key found in public is leaked whatever the user says. The policy is the start of the response.

choices.text: Deactivating, investigating and rotating, as for any leaked key
choices.why: Right. The quarantine blocks the costly and persistent actions; it undoes nothing and AWS still says to rotate.

choices.text: Attaching version `V2` as well, since each version covers different services
choices.why: A later version replaces an earlier one; stacking them adds nothing that the response needs.

prompt: Which tool refuses a commit containing an AWS key on the developer's own laptop, before any server sees it?
hint: It installs hooks in the local repository.

choices.text: GitHub's push protection
choices.why: Push protection refuses the push at GitHub, after the commit already exists on the laptop.

choices.text: `git-secrets`, from AWS Labs
choices.why: Right. Its hooks check each commit's changes against AWS's key patterns.

choices.text: The credential report
choices.why: The report lists keys that exist in IAM; it knows nothing of anybody's repository.

choices.text: The `AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3` policy
choices.why: That is applied after a key is found in public, which is exactly what the question wants to prevent.

prompt: The shop's GitHub Actions deploy signs with an IAM user's key stored as a repository secret, and `key-ages.py` flags it at 200 days. What is the better fix?
hint: Is this one of the cases where a key is unavoidable?

choices.text: Rotate it now and put a reminder every 90 days
choices.why: That keeps a key where none is needed. A pipeline with an OIDC token is not on the last-resort list.

choices.text: Trade the workflow's OIDC token for `deployer`; delete the key
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10's web identity: short sessions, a `sub` condition naming the repository, and no secret to age.

choices.text: Move the key from the repository's secrets to the organisation's
choices.why: The key would then be readable by more repositories, not fewer, and just as old.

choices.text: Require MFA on the user with a `BoolIfExists` condition
choices.why: A pipeline has no phone to give a code. The condition would simply stop every deploy.

prompt: An alert says `erp-sync`'s current key appeared in a public paste an hour ago. Which command does `ana` type first?
hint: Reversible, and immediate.

choices.text: `aws iam delete-user --user-name erp-sync`
choices.why: IAM refuses to delete a user that still has keys and policies, and success would lose the record of what the key was.

choices.text: `aws iam create-access-key --user-name erp-sync`
choices.why: A new key keeps the program running, and leaves the leaked one working for the stranger meanwhile.

choices.text: `aws iam update-access-key --user-name erp-sync --access-key-id … --status Inactive`
choices.why: Right. It stops the key at once and can be reversed; the investigation and the rotation come after.

choices.text: `aws iam generate-credential-report`
choices.why: The report describes keys and stops none of them. It can wait until the key is off.

prompt: Match each command to its step in a rotation.
hint: Four steps, four commands.

pairs.right: checking the old key went quiet
the step that cannot be undone

right_distractors: moving the program to the new key

prompt: Of the shop's callers, which one does the lesson leave with an access key, and why that one?
hint: Outside AWS, with no certificate and no browser.

choices.text: `bia`, because developers need the command line every day
choices.why: People have Identity Center and `aws sso login`, lesson 11. People are not on the list.

choices.text: The web servers, because they read `shop-assets` constantly
choices.why: They run on EC2 and wear `shop-app` through an instance profile, lesson 10.

choices.text: `erp-sync`, the office's accounting system
choices.why: Right. A program outside AWS that the shop cannot give a certificate to, calling on a schedule: the short list that is left.

choices.text: The deploy pipeline, because CI runs outside AWS
choices.why: It runs outside AWS and still has an OIDC token to trade for a role.
